extracted.intended_audience: stage magicians, theatrical performers, and theatre managers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and standards for mounting, presenting, and managing stage magic/illusion performances — covering timing, staging, publicity, audience management, contingency handling, and ethical considerations. Drawn from a performer's memoir but framed as actionable principles for producing successful séances/varieté magic shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactitude (punctuality and adherence to schedule)
rubrics_metrics.description: «je vous recommande l’exactitude.» Performances, openings, reprises and inventions must be finished and presented at the precise hour and date promised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative emphasizes starting at appointed times (e.g., the King’s four o’clock), finishing inventions by set deadlines (reopening fixed at 1 September) and the importance of being able to resume performances on advertised dates; lateness or missed engagements risks audience ire and professional harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance imperturbable (stage confidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate an unflappable assurance and self-confidence gained from repeated successful sessions: 'Grâce à mes nombreuses séances, j’avais ... une assurance imperturbable'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence steadies performance and convinces spectators; this comes from practice and consistent successful execution. Present with calm control to strengthen perceived credibility of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide the audience’s attention and reactions (dramatic build)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the effect to grow progressively — start to direct audience silence and then increase communicativeness up to expressive demonstrations and bravos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'suspension éthérée' is divided into three points (remove stool → remove one cane → lift to horizontal) so astonishment escalates stepwise. Design acts so each phase raises stakes and guides applause/tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realistic precautions and verifications to strengthen effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage visible checks (e.g., sending people to guard the orange tree) so later discoveries seem impossible and thus more impressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow or stage audience inspection/guarding of targets, which, even if belated, enhances credibility of the result and increases theatrical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create convincing backstory and physical evidence for illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ sealed documents, aged seals, signatures and dated parchments (example: cassette with Cagliostro’s signature) to supply authoritative-looking proof for a trick’s impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-crafted props and narratives (old seals, certificates) make a routine extraordinary; attention to provenance details persuades skeptical viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough preparation and rehearsal of performers (including child actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train assistants and child performers carefully so they can execute roles flawlessly—even at a young age ('mon fils ... le joua avec une telle perfection').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex effects demand rehearsed timing and familiarity with cues. Early instruction and role practice reduce onstage errors and increase believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical awareness and audience sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of ethical perceptions (some considered the 'éthérisation' of a child inhumane and threatened legal action); anticipate and respond to audience moral concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design effects to avoid genuine harm or appearance of cruelty; when a routine could be misread, prepare explanations or safeguards to reassure public and authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency management and candid audience communication
rubrics_metrics.description: If mishaps occur (injury, missing prop, late entrance), explain succinctly and honestly to the audience to regain sympathy and silence hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative example: after falling into a trap, the performer returned, recounted the accident (paleness proved truth), which disarmed the crowd. Quick, sincere explanation and visible evidence of distress can convert boos into applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage safety and crew protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dismiss essential stage personnel (regisseur, machiniste); verify trapdoors and stage openings before performances to avoid accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's accident (trapillon left open) resulted from absence of necessary crew and checks. Maintain a checklist and leave critical crew in place even if trying to minimize staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renew repertoire and innovate continually
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly invent and renew acts to maintain public interest; do not rely solely on past successes ('Croire tout découvert est une erreur profonde; Je ferai du nouveau').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New apparatus and refreshed sequences are necessary to sustain vogue; plan inventions and complete them in time for scheduled reopening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity, decor and presentation matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in advertising and stage presentation (large posters, rich decor, a curtain with golden title) to attract and frame the show appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In London the director ordered a Louis XV salon set and a curtain with the show title in gold; a visually striking setting helps audience expectations and ticket sales. Use dedicated publicity managers (e.g., Nemmo) to handle announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate sensible theatre terms and respect co-production constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When alternating with other companies, agree on suitable days, revenue shares, expense responsibilities, and respect rehearsal/occupation schedules (clear stage promptly, take allotted midday slot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author accepted alternating performances with opera-comique (Tues/Thurs/Sat), sharing gross receipts and covering expenses; clear contractual expectations reduce friction and fatigue from logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage patrons and endorsements but recognize their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal or influential attendance and private protectors can boost reception (ovations, filled halls) but may not fully create lasting vogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use endorsements to gain initial momentum (royal boxes, protectors recommending you), but continue to earn public favor through quality acts; be aware some applause may be solicited rather than spontaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with gratuitous tickets (billets de faveur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Free tickets often attract indifferent or inhibited audiences who may not applaud and can harm atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observed that recipients of free tickets rarely support the show with applause and may even reduce perceived value. Limit gratuitous distribution or use it strategically to avoid dead air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subtle managerial discretion in staffing and hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat artists and staff with delicacy and generosity (e.g., providing prized lodgings or access to good boxes) to cultivate goodwill and reciprocal support from theatre directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal courtesy from managers (Mitchell’s provision of a loge) fosters cooperative relationships; kindness and fair dealing are practical investments in career longevity.
